A comprehensive analysis of Indian pompano (Trachinotus mookalee) reveals a robust set of life-history parameters that situate this carangid within a moderately fast life-history continuum. The fertilised eggs, with a diameter of approximately 1 mm, give rise to yolk-sac larvae that have an estimated dry weight at birth of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a value derived from the geometric relationship of the spherical egg volume. At a stable rearing temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], the newly hatched prolarvae are classified as endotrophic larvae, subsisting entirely on endogenous yolk reserves. The time from fertilisation to eclosion is remarkably brief, with the age at birth recorded at 3.2 days [ab = 3.2 days] under these thermal conditions, a duration consistent with the rapid embryonic development observed in many warm-water carangids at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This short incubation period reflects the energetic advantages of elevated water temperatures during early ontogeny, facilitating a swift transition from the chorionate embryo to the free-swimming, yolk-dependent larva.

Field surveys and captive rearing studies have collectively documented the species' remarkable capacity for somatic growth, with the largest individuals achieving an ultimate fork length of 90 centimeters [Li = 90 centimeters]. This asymptotic size is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 8300 grams [Wwi = 8300 grams], a mass that aligns closely with length-weight relationships established for congeneric species such as Trachinotus falcatus. The attainment of such substantial body dimensions, however, is not immediate; the trajectory from a recently metamorphosed juvenile to a fully grown adult spans many years. A critical milestone along this developmental pathway is the onset of sexual maturation, which occurs at a fork length at puberty of 45 centimeters [Lp = 45 centimeters], indicating that individuals must reach approximately half their ultimate length before initiating gonadal development. This allometric relationship between size and reproductive maturity is a common theme among iteroparous marine fishes.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) is approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] when measured at a water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. Further refinement of this parameter through direct field sampling of wild populations of Trachinotus mookalee would be valuable, particularly given the influence of local environmental conditions and prey availability on gonadal recrudescence. Such data would strengthen comparative analyses within the Carangidae family.

Longevity estimates for Indian pompano, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age determination, point to a maximum lifespan of approximately 8395 days [am = approximately 8395 days] under natural conditions at a sustained water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This extended life history places the species among the longer-lived members of its genus and reflects a life-history strategy that balances moderate early mortality with extended reproductive opportunities across multiple seasons. The senescence pattern in this species appears to be gradual, with no evidence of a sudden post-reproductive mortality event characteristic of semelparous fishes. Instead, adult mortality increases progressively with age, driven likely by the cumulative physiological costs of annual spawning migrations and the energetic demands of maintaining a large body mass. This longevity is a key parameter for population viability models and fisheries management strategies.

The demersal eggs of Indian pompano, each measuring approximately 1 mm in diameter, represent a substantial initial energetic investment given their dry weight of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. The gonadosomatic index was approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. At the population level, these life-history traits — the rapid yolk-sac larval phase, the moderate GSI, the late maturity at 45 centimeters [Lp = 45 centimeters] fork length, and the substantial ultimate body size of 90 centimeters [Li = 90 centimeters] culminating in a wet weight of 8300 grams [Wwi = 8300 grams] — collectively describe a species that balances early growth with extended reproductive tenure. Comparative data from other carangids suggest that this combination of traits is well-suited to stable, productive coastal environments where food resources are predictable, allowing individuals to reach large sizes and invest in multiple spawning events over an extended lifespan at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C].
